title: "Coefficients And Estimators"

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(misskappa)
```

## Coefficients

Agreement coefficients in `misskappa` are written in terms of pairwise
disagreement. For two raters with categorical ratings in
$\{1,\ldots,C\}$, let $L$ be a loss matrix with
$\ell_{cc}=0$ and $0 \le \ell_{cd} \le 1$. The generic coefficient is

$$
\kappa = 1 - \frac{D_o}{D_e},
$$

where $D_o$ is observed disagreement and $D_e$ is the disagreement
expected under a chance model. Different named coefficients mostly differ in
how they estimate these two quantities when there are more than two raters.

For a subject $i$ and raters $r,s$, complete-data pairwise
disagreement is

$$
d_{irs} = \ell_{X_{ir}, X_{is}}.
$$

Observed disagreement $D_o$ averages $d_{irs}$ over subjects and rater pairs.
The coefficients differ in the chance model behind $D_e$: Conger pairs each
rater's own category distribution, Fleiss pools the raters' distributions,
and Brennan-Prediger draws uniformly from the rating scale, so it needs that
scale to be known (declare it with `categories` when some categories went
unused).

The `weight` argument picks the loss: `"nominal"` ($\ell_{cd}=1$ for
$c \neq d$), or `"linear"` and `"quadratic"` for ordered categories, scaled by
the range of the category scores $v$. The quadratic loss is

$$
\ell_{cd} =
\frac{(v_c - v_d)^2}{(\max_j v_j - \min_j v_j)^2},
$$

and lets the
coefficient be expressed through the rater means and covariance matrix, which
is what the scored estimators `"pairwise"`, `"nt_fiml"`, and `"nt_fiml_cs"`
exploit: they estimate those moments under missing data and map them to the
coefficients.

## Estimators under missing data

The estimators split into moment estimators, consistent when ratings are
missing completely at random (MCAR), and likelihood estimators, consistent
when missingness may depend on the observed ratings (MAR). `NA` marks a
missing rating.

The simplest moment estimator averages the loss over the observed rater
pairs:

$$
\widehat D_o =
\frac{\sum_i \sum_{r<s} R_{ir}R_{is}
  \ell_{X_{ir},X_{is}}}
{\sum_i \sum_{r<s} R_{ir}R_{is}},
$$

where $R_{ir}=1$ when the rating is observed. Pooling pairs this way weights
each rater pair by how often it is co-observed. That is harmless when raters
share an observation rate, but with rater-varying rates and non-exchangeable
raters it targets a different average than the fixed-rater coefficient.

The IPW estimator (`"ipw"`) corrects this by reweighting observed pairs by
estimated observation probabilities. In schematic form,

$$
\widehat D_o^{\mathrm{IPW}} =
\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \sum_{r<s}
\frac{R_{ir}R_{is}}{\widehat\pi_r\widehat\pi_s}
\ell_{X_{ir},X_{is}},
$$

with corresponding weighted marginal estimates for chance disagreement. This
is the default and recommended estimator for categorical ratings. The scored `"pairwise"`
estimator takes a different route to the same goal: it estimates each rater
mean and each pairwise covariance from the subjects who observed it, and the
quadratic coefficients are functions of those moments, so it is consistent
under MCAR.

The categorical FIML estimator (`"cat_fiml"`) fits a categorical full-data
distribution under MAR by EM.
For observed pattern $o_i$, the likelihood contribution is

$$
L_i(\theta) =
\sum_{x_{\mathrm{mis}}}
p_\theta(x_{\mathrm{obs},i}, x_{\mathrm{mis}}),
$$

and agreement coefficients are computed from the fitted full-data
distribution. The implementation returns Wald covariance estimates through
Louis' observed information when available.

For scored (quadratically weighted) ratings the normal-theory FIML fits a
Gaussian mean and covariance by EM and reads the coefficient off the fitted
moments with a sandwich delta-method standard error. Two covariance models are
available, selected by the estimator name: `"nt_fiml"` fits a *saturated*
covariance, while `"nt_fiml_cs"` fits the *compound-symmetry*
$\Sigma = \psi J + e I$ (the fixed-rater variance-component model, with free
rater means). Compound symmetry needs only a connected co-observation graph and
is consistent and slightly more efficient when that structure holds, and is
robust under MCAR even when the covariance is misspecified. The saturated model
is the safer choice under MAR when the covariance may depart from compound
symmetry.

### Compound symmetry on a planned-incomplete design

The saturated coefficients (`"pairwise"`, `"nt_fiml"`, `"cat_fiml"`) are
functions of *every* pairwise second moment, so they are identified only when
every rater pair is jointly observed by some subject, a *complete*
co-observation graph. The compound-symmetry estimator needs only a *connected*
graph, and that is the whole point of a planned-incomplete design: you can rate
each subject with a rotating subset of raters and still recover the coefficient.

The synthetic `dat.tenhove2025` data (60 subjects, 6 raters, ordinal `1`--`5`)
is such a design, in the style of the planned-incomplete ICC studies of ten Hove
et al. (2025). Each subject is rated by three of the six raters in overlapping
panels, so the graph is connected but some pairs (raters 2 and 4, for example)
never co-occur:

```{r}
# Each subject has exactly three of the six ratings.
table(rowSums(is.finite(dat.tenhove2025)))

# Off-diagonal zeros are rater pairs that never rate the same subject.
co <- crossprod(is.finite(dat.tenhove2025))
diag(co) <- 0
co
```

Asking for a saturated coefficient on this pattern stops with an
identifiability error before the estimator runs:

```{r}
#| error: true
agreement(dat.tenhove2025, estimator = "nt_fiml")
```

The compound-symmetry estimator fits the same data. Declaring the `1`--`5`
scale adds Brennan-Prediger to Conger and Fleiss:

```{r}
agreement(dat.tenhove2025, estimator = "nt_fiml_cs", categories = 1:5)
```

All three coefficients come with sandwich standard errors, recovered from a
design where the saturated estimators cannot be computed at all.

Brennan, R. L., & Prediger, D. J. (1981). Coefficient kappa: Some uses,
misuses, and alternatives. *Educational and Psychological Measurement*,
41(3), 687–699.

Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. *Educational
and Psychological Measurement*, 20(1), 37–46.

Cohen, J. (1968). Weighted kappa: Nominal scale agreement with provision for
scaled disagreement or partial credit. *Psychological Bulletin*, 70(4),
213–220.

Conger, A. J. (1980). Integration and generalization of kappas for multiple
raters. *Psychological Bulletin*, 88(2), 322–328.

*Psychological Bulletin*, 76(5), 378–382.

ICCs for interrater reliability from planned incomplete data. *Multivariate
Behavioral Research*, 60(5). <https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2025.2507745>
